youtube.aciklama:
Configuration is the shape that thresholds trace across frequency on the audiogram. In this lesson, we use sample audiograms to look at flat, rising, sloping and precipitously sloping configurations, the 4 kHz notch, and the cookie-bite and reverse cookie-bite shapes, and we discuss how to describe them in a report.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Lloyd and Kaplan, Audiometric Interpretation: A Manual of Basic Audiometry; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; Gelfand, Essentials of Audiology; ASHA, Guidelines for Manual Pure-Tone Threshold Audiometry (2005).

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson, we learn to recognize and correctly name the shape of the audiogram, its configuration.
We will see each configuration on a sample audiogram and discuss how to describe it in a report.
When describing an audiogram, we look at four features: the degree, type and configuration of the loss, and the symmetry between the ears.
Configuration is the shape that the thresholds trace across frequency, in other words, the form of the audiogram curve.
As we saw in earlier lessons, degree and type tell us how much loss there is and where it comes from.
Configuration shows which frequencies the loss is concentrated in.
Two losses of the same degree can cause very different difficulties in daily life if their configurations differ.
Configuration helps us predict how a loss will affect daily life.
For example, the same average threshold can cause very different speech problems in a flat loss and in a steeply sloping loss.
Because the pure tone average includes only a few frequencies, it can hide this difference.
Configuration also gives clues to possible causes and guides hearing aid fitting.
Configurations are classified by how much the thresholds change per octave.
If thresholds change by less than five decibels per octave, the configuration is flat.
If thresholds improve by more than five decibels per octave toward the high frequencies, we speak of a rising configuration.
If thresholds worsen by about five to twelve decibels per octave, it is called gradually sloping.
If the worsening is about fifteen to twenty decibels per octave, it is called sharply sloping.
If there is a drop of twenty five decibels or more per octave after a certain frequency, it is called precipitously sloping.
These limits are based on the widely used classification of Lloyd and Kaplan; sources may differ slightly.
In a flat configuration, thresholds are close to one another at all frequencies.
In this example, the right ear thresholds are between forty five and fifty five dB HL and form an almost horizontal line.
A flat configuration is common in conductive losses such as otitis media with effusion.
A flat curve can also be seen in some sensorineural losses.
In a flat loss, all frequencies of speech are turned down to a similar degree.
That is why, especially in flat conductive losses, making sound louder often brings clear benefit.
In a sloping, or falling, configuration, thresholds get steadily worse as frequency rises.
In this example, the threshold is twenty dB HL at two hundred fifty hertz and drops to sixty five dB HL at eight thousand hertz.
It is one of the most common configurations in adults.
Age-related hearing loss typically appears as a symmetric curve in both ears, falling toward the high frequencies.
These people hear vowels but miss high-pitched consonants; we saw this in detail with the speech banana.
Where the slope begins and how steep it is also affect how much gain is given at each frequency in hearing aid fitting.
In this example, thresholds are within normal limits up to one thousand hertz.
Between one thousand and two thousand hertz, however, the threshold drops by thirty five decibels at once.
This sudden drop after a certain frequency is called a precipitously sloping configuration.
In such losses, the region of the drop may contain areas where the cochlea barely functions; these are called cochlear dead regions.
Testing interoctave frequencies where the drop occurs, for example fifteen hundred hertz, clarifies the shape of the curve.
Because their low frequencies are good, these people sometimes notice their loss late.
In a rising configuration, the loss is greater at low frequencies, and thresholds improve toward the high frequencies.
This shape is much rarer than a falling configuration.
For example, a low-frequency sensorineural loss can be seen in the early stage of Meniere's disease.
Some conductive problems that increase middle ear stiffness can also affect the low frequencies more.
None of these examples establishes a diagnosis on its own; configuration is only a clue.
A notch is a dip in threshold in a certain frequency region, followed by recovery.
In this example, both ears show a clear dip at four thousand hertz.
At eight thousand hertz, the thresholds improve again; this is called recovery.
A notch like this between three thousand and six thousand hertz is typical of noise-induced hearing loss.
The exact location of the notch varies between people; it can appear at three thousand, four thousand or six thousand hertz.
In this example, the finding is a clue that calls for a detailed noise history; a diagnosis is not made from the audiogram alone.
Another notch, seen in bone conduction around two thousand hertz, the Carhart notch, is linked to otosclerosis; we cover it separately.
In a cookie-bite configuration, the loss is concentrated in the mid frequencies, while the low and high frequencies are better.
On the audiogram, it forms a U shape, as if a bite had been taken out of the middle of the curve.
In this example, thresholds are fifty dB HL at one thousand and two thousand hertz, and about twenty to twenty five dB HL at the ends.
This configuration is often associated with hereditary sensorineural losses.
Because the mid frequencies matter for speech, the person may struggle to understand speech even though the outer frequencies are good.

maddeler.metin: Poor at the ends, _better_ in the middle

cumleler: The reverse cookie-bite is the opposite: the low and high frequencies are poor, and the mid frequencies are better.
On the audiogram, it forms an inverted U shape.
It is a rare configuration in general clinical practice.
Lloyd and Kaplan call this a peaked audiogram; it is often reported in Meniere's disease, but it is not specific to it.
With unexpected shapes like this, it is also important to recheck the results to rule out measurement error.
After describing the configuration, we compare the two ears.
If the threshold difference between the ears is small, the loss is considered symmetric.
Sources use different criteria for asymmetry, for example a difference of fifteen decibels or more at two or more frequencies.
A clear and unexplained asymmetry is noted as a finding that may need further evaluation.
Together, configuration and symmetry complete the picture of the loss.
Now let us see all the configurations together.
The links in the table are only possible examples; the same configuration can arise from different causes.
Configuration gains meaning together with the history, the type of loss and other tests.
Writing the degree, type, configuration and symmetry together in the report makes the information clear to everyone who reads it.
For example: symmetric, mild to moderate, sloping sensorineural hearing loss in both ears.

sahneler.metin: If adjacent octaves differ by 20 dB or more, test the interoctave frequencies too; if 6000 Hz is skipped, a noise notch can be missed.
cumleler: A tip from practice: octave frequencies alone may not be enough to see the configuration correctly.
If adjacent octaves differ by twenty decibels or more, test the interoctave frequencies too.
If six thousand hertz in particular is skipped, a noise-induced notch can be missed.
Three thousand hertz clarifies where a steep drop begins and covers a region that matters for speech.
Configuration is the shape the thresholds trace across frequency, and it is described with degree, type and symmetry.
By slope, we distinguish flat, rising, sloping and precipitously sloping configurations.
A four thousand hertz notch with recovery at eight thousand hertz calls for questions about noise history.
In a cookie-bite, the loss is in the mid frequencies; in a reverse cookie-bite, it is at the outer frequencies.

sahneler.aciklama: A shape that dips in one region and then recovers is a _notch_; it calls for questions about noise history.
